Done. Here’s what I set up:

1) Canary deployment
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
- Replicas: 2
- Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Container name/port/security: matched stable (rec-engine, containerPort: 80, no explicit securityContext)

2) Traffic split (~50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select only app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
- Kept Service port mapping the same (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Current state
- Stable engine-v2-0: 2 replicas available
- Canary engine-v2-1: 2 replicas available
- With 4 total pods and equal replica counts, the Service will load-balance roughly 50% of traffic to the canary.

Notes
- The Service uses targetPort 8080; the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. The containerPort field (80) is metadata and does not affect actual listening ports; I matched it to the stable deployment as requested.
- To rollback the canary from the Service: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0. To remove the canary entirely: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
- Replicas: 2
- Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Container name/port/security: matched stable (rec-engine, containerPort: 80, no explicit securityContext)

2) Traffic split (~50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select only app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
- Kept Service port mapping the same (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Current state
- Stable engine-v2-0: 2 replicas available
- Canary engine-v2-1: 2 replicas available
- With 4 total pods and equal replica counts, the Service will load-balance roughly 50% of traffic to the canary.

Notes
- The Service uses targetPort 8080; the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. The containerPort field (80) is metadata and does not affect actual listening ports; I matched it to the stable deployment as requested.
- To rollback the canary from the Service: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0. To remove the canary entirely: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

outputSteps.content:
Done. Here’s what I set up:

1) Canary deployment
- Created Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
- Replicas: 2
- Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
- Container name/port/security: matched stable (rec-engine, containerPort: 80, no explicit securityContext)

2) Traffic split (~50/50)
- Updated Service recommendation-engine to select only app: recommendation-engine (removed version filter)
- Kept Service port mapping the same (port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080)

Current state
- Stable engine-v2-0: 2 replicas available
- Canary engine-v2-1: 2 replicas available
- With 4 total pods and equal replica counts, the Service will load-balance roughly 50% of traffic to the canary.

Notes
- The Service uses targetPort 8080; the nginx-unprivileged image listens on 8080 by default. The containerPort field (80) is metadata and does not affect actual listening ports; I matched it to the stable deployment as requested.
- To rollback the canary from the Service: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.0. To remove the canary entirely: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

results.taskOutput:
Fix applied.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overridden the image entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing the pod to crash and back-off.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs.
- Kept the same image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) and exposed containerPort 8080, which that image uses.

Current status
- A new ReplicaSet was created and the old one scaled down.
- Pod in crashloop-test is now Running: app-5c7bd5bd8f-8w9rm (1/1 Ready, 0 restarts).

If you want, I can also create a Service to expose port 8080.

Steps.message:
Fix applied.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overridden the image entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing the pod to crash and back-off.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs.
- Kept the same image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) and exposed containerPort 8080, which that image uses.

Current status
- A new ReplicaSet was created and the old one scaled down.
- Pod in crashloop-test is now Running: app-5c7bd5bd8f-8w9rm (1/1 Ready, 0 restarts).

If you want, I can also create a Service to expose port 8080.

  namespace: crashloop-test

  replicas: 1

outputSteps.content:
Fix applied.

What was wrong
- The Deployment overridden the image entrypoint with: /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing the pod to crash and back-off.

What I changed
- Removed the custom command/args so the image’s default entrypoint runs.
- Kept the same image (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged) and exposed containerPort 8080, which that image uses.

Current status
- A new ReplicaSet was created and the old one scaled down.
- Pod in crashloop-test is now Running: app-5c7bd5bd8f-8w9rm (1/1 Ready, 0 restarts).

If you want, I can also create a Service to expose port 8080.

results.taskOutput:
I found why homepage-pod was Pending: it was waiting on PVC homepage-pvc, which was Pending because it referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Available storage classes are "standard" (default) and "csi-hostpath-sc".

What I changed
- Deleted the broken PVC homepage-pvc (it had no bound PV, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is up.

Notes
- If you intended to use a specific StorageClass named "sc", let me know and I can create it or switch the PVC to it.
- In the future, you can omit storageClassName to use the cluster’s default class.

namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found why homepage-pod was Pending: it was waiting on PVC homepage-pvc, which was Pending because it referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Available storage classes are "standard" (default) and "csi-hostpath-sc".

What I changed
- Deleted the broken PVC homepage-pvc (it had no bound PV, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is up.

Notes
- If you intended to use a specific StorageClass named "sc", let me know and I can create it or switch the PVC to it.
- In the future, you can omit storageClassName to use the cluster’s default class.

outputSteps.content:
I found why homepage-pod was Pending: it was waiting on PVC homepage-pvc, which was Pending because it referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc". Available storage classes are "standard" (default) and "csi-hostpath-sc".

What I changed
- Deleted the broken PVC homepage-pvc (it had no bound PV, so no data loss).
- Recreated homepage-pvc with storageClassName: standard and 1Gi RWO.

Current status
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi).
- Pod homepage-pod: Running and Ready on node mcp-eval-cluster. Container nginx is up.

Notes
- If you intended to use a specific StorageClass named "sc", let me know and I can create it or switch the PVC to it.
- In the future, you can omit storageClassName to use the cluster’s default class.

results.taskOutput:
It’s fixed.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking port 80 at non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 listed; harmless).
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 and named the port http.

Current state
- Pod orders/webapp-7c9c694bf6-pqgs7: 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints: webapp → 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return NGINX welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080.

Do you want this exposed externally (Ingress/Route or LoadBalancer)? If you share a hostname, I can create an Ingress for you.

apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
  labels:
    app: webapp
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: webapp
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80
    targetPort: 8080
    protocol: TCP

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: webapp
  namespace: orders
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: webapp
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: webapp
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: webapp
        image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
          protocol: TCP
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 3
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 3
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /
            port: 8080
            scheme: HTTP
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 2
          failureThreshold: 3

namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

It’s fixed.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking port 80 at non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 listed; harmless).
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 and named the port http.

Current state
- Pod orders/webapp-7c9c694bf6-pqgs7: 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints: webapp → 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return NGINX welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080.

Do you want this exposed externally (Ingress/Route or LoadBalancer)? If you share a hostname, I can create an Ingress for you.

outputSteps.content:
It’s fixed.

What was wrong
- The container image (nginx-unprivileged) listens on port 8080, but:
  - Probes were checking port 80 at non-existent paths (/get_status and /is_ready), causing restarts.
  - The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Deployment:
  - Updated readiness and liveness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
  - Exposed container port 8080 (kept 80 listed; harmless).
- Service:
  - Set targetPort to 8080 and named the port http.

Current state
- Pod orders/webapp-7c9c694bf6-pqgs7: 1/1 Running, Ready.
- Service endpoints: webapp → 10.244.0.25:8080.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/ (should return NGINX welcome page).
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080.

Do you want this exposed externally (Ingress/Route or LoadBalancer)? If you share a hostname, I can create an Ingress for you.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause:
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1), not pods (core/v1). So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core API pods:

outputSteps.content:
Root cause:
- The Role bound to your pod-reader service account only allowed listing deployments (apps/v1), not pods (core/v1). So the SA lacked permission to list pods in simple-rbac-setup.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core API pods:
  - resources: pods
  - verbs: get, list, watch
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader, so no changes were needed there.

You can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace using that service account.

How to verify:
- If you have kubectl access, run:
  - kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
  - or impersonate to fetch: kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Note:
- This permission is namespace-scoped. To list pods in other namespaces, you'd need a Role in each namespace or a ClusterRole with a ClusterRoleBinding.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints. 
  - Service selector was app=web
  - NGINX Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
- Because of the mismatch, the nginx Service routed to zero backends and wasn’t reachable.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web to use selector app=nginx. After this change, Endpoints for the Service populated with the nginx Pod IP on port 8080.

Verification
- Launched a temporary test client Pod in web and fetched http://nginx (ClusterIP Service). It returned the default “Welcome to nginx!” page, confirming the Service now works inside the cluster.

What this means for access
- Currently the Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). It’s reachable from within the cluster (e.g., other Pods) but not from outside.
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a port on each node
  - LoadBalancer: if your environment supports it (e.g., cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: if you have an Ingress controller installed

Tell me which exposure you prefer and any hostname/port requirements, and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I created a small test Pod (test-client) to verify connectivity. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints. 
  - Service selector was app=web
  - NGINX Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
- Because of the mismatch, the nginx Service routed to zero backends and wasn’t reachable.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web to use selector app=nginx. After this change, Endpoints for the Service populated with the nginx Pod IP on port 8080.

Verification
- Launched a temporary test client Pod in web and fetched http://nginx (ClusterIP Service). It returned the default “Welcome to nginx!” page, confirming the Service now works inside the cluster.

What this means for access
- Currently the Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). It’s reachable from within the cluster (e.g., other Pods) but not from outside.
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a port on each node
  - LoadBalancer: if your environment supports it (e.g., cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: if you have an Ingress controller installed

Tell me which exposure you prefer and any hostname/port requirements, and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I created a small test Pod (test-client) to verify connectivity. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Root cause: The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels, so the Service had no endpoints. 
  - Service selector was app=web
  - NGINX Deployment/Pod labels are app=nginx
- Because of the mismatch, the nginx Service routed to zero backends and wasn’t reachable.

Fix applied
- Updated the Service in namespace web to use selector app=nginx. After this change, Endpoints for the Service populated with the nginx Pod IP on port 8080.

Verification
- Launched a temporary test client Pod in web and fetched http://nginx (ClusterIP Service). It returned the default “Welcome to nginx!” page, confirming the Service now works inside the cluster.

What this means for access
- Currently the Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). It’s reachable from within the cluster (e.g., other Pods) but not from outside.
- If you need external access, choose one:
  - NodePort: expose on a port on each node
  - LoadBalancer: if your environment supports it (e.g., cloud or MetalLB)
  - Ingress: if you have an Ingress controller installed

Tell me which exposure you prefer and any hostname/port requirements, and I’ll set it up.

Optional cleanup
- I created a small test Pod (test-client) to verify connectivity. Say the word and I’ll remove it.

results.taskOutput:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” leaving the pods Pending and the Service with no endpoints.
- Additionally, the Service was targeting port 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image serves on 8080 by default. Even after the pods came up, this mismatch would have caused a connection failure.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service to target port 8080 to match the nginx-unprivileged container.

Current status (verified)
- Deployment: web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas.
- Pods: Running and Ready:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vxb6j
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-c229m
- Service: web-app-service has healthy endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080
- Container logs show NGINX started cleanly.

Impact
- The “connection refused” error occurred because there were no Service endpoints (pods Pending). With pods now running and the Service targeting the correct port, calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

If you actually need to pin these pods to special nodes
- Either re-add the nodeSelector and label a node accordingly: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or replace nodeSelector with a toleration/affinity policy that matches your intended nodes.

Optional follow-ups
- Add a readinessProbe on port 8080 so the Service only routes to ready containers.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for stability.

Want me to add a readiness probe and resource limits, or label a node if you do require the production-gpu placement?

Steps.message:
namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” leaving the pods Pending and the Service with no endpoints.
- Additionally, the Service was targeting port 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image serves on 8080 by default. Even after the pods came up, this mismatch would have caused a connection failure.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service to target port 8080 to match the nginx-unprivileged container.

Current status (verified)
- Deployment: web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas.
- Pods: Running and Ready:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vxb6j
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-c229m
- Service: web-app-service has healthy endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080
- Container logs show NGINX started cleanly.

Impact
- The “connection refused” error occurred because there were no Service endpoints (pods Pending). With pods now running and the Service targeting the correct port, calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

If you actually need to pin these pods to special nodes
- Either re-add the nodeSelector and label a node accordingly: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or replace nodeSelector with a toleration/affinity policy that matches your intended nodes.

Optional follow-ups
- Add a readinessProbe on port 8080 so the Service only routes to ready containers.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for stability.

Want me to add a readiness probe and resource limits, or label a node if you do require the production-gpu placement?

outputSteps.content:
Here’s what I found and what I fixed.

What was wrong
- Pods weren’t running due to an invalid nodeSelector. The Deployment had spec.template.spec.nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but no node in the cluster has that label. Scheduler events showed “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector,” leaving the pods Pending and the Service with no endpoints.
- Additionally, the Service was targeting port 80 while the nginx-unprivileged image serves on 8080 by default. Even after the pods came up, this mismatch would have caused a connection failure.

What I changed
- Removed the nodeSelector so pods can schedule on the available node.
- Updated the Service to target port 8080 to match the nginx-unprivileged container.

Current status (verified)
- Deployment: web-app-deployment is Available with 2/2 replicas.
- Pods: Running and Ready:
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-vxb6j
  - web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-c229m
- Service: web-app-service has healthy endpoints:
  - 10.244.0.33:8080
  - 10.244.0.34:8080
- Container logs show NGINX started cleanly.

Impact
- The “connection refused” error occurred because there were no Service endpoints (pods Pending). With pods now running and the Service targeting the correct port, calls to http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local:80 should succeed.

If you actually need to pin these pods to special nodes
- Either re-add the nodeSelector and label a node accordingly: kubectl label node <node-name> environment=production-gpu
- Or replace nodeSelector with a toleration/affinity policy that matches your intended nodes.

Optional follow-ups
- Add a readinessProbe on port 8080 so the Service only routes to ready containers.
- Consider pinning to a specific image tag instead of latest for stability.

Want me to add a readiness probe and resource limits, or label a node if you do require the production-gpu placement?

Steps.message:
Done. I created the Pod communication-pod in the multi-container-logging namespace with:
- Containers:
  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged, serving on port 8080
  - logger: busybox:latest, command: sh -c 'tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log'
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir), mounted at /var/log/nginx in both containers
- Readiness: HTTP readinessProbe on the web-server (GET / on port 8080), so the Pod is ready when the web server is serving traffic

You can verify:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger -f (to see tailed access logs)

results.taskOutput:
All requested resources have been created and applied. Summary of what’s set up:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Labels added (e.g., ns: <namespace>) to support NetworkPolicy selectors

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings (namespace-admin) bind:
    - User alice → dev-alice (ClusterRole admin)
    - User bob → dev-bob (ClusterRole admin)
    - User charlie → dev-charlie (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (dev-readers) in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (accessible only to cluster-admins)
- ServiceAccounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only in dev-shared

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace + DNS/system services:
  - In each namespace above: allow ingress from same namespace, and egress to:
    - Same namespace pods
    - kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Dev access to dev-shared only:
  - In each dev namespace: egress allowed to namespaceSelector ns=dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: ingress allowed from namespaces with ns in {dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie}
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No egress from dev namespaces to staging/prod
  - Staging/prod only intra-namespace + DNS egress; no cross-env traffic

5) Default Deny Coverage
- Applied to all non-system namespaces; no policies added to kube-system or other system namespaces

Notes and verification
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-K, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebindings,sa,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings,resourcequota,networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy; kubectl -n prod get networkpolicy
- ServiceAccount tokens: on Kubernetes 1.24+, use projected tokens (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or set up workload mounts as needed.

If you want, I can export all applied manifests in a single YAML bundle for version control.

Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested resources have been created and applied. Summary of what’s set up:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Labels added (e.g., ns: <namespace>) to support NetworkPolicy selectors

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings (namespace-admin) bind:
    - User alice → dev-alice (ClusterRole admin)
    - User bob → dev-bob (ClusterRole admin)
    - User charlie → dev-charlie (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (dev-readers) in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (accessible only to cluster-admins)
- ServiceAccounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only in dev-shared

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace + DNS/system services:
  - In each namespace above: allow ingress from same namespace, and egress to:
    - Same namespace pods
    - kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Dev access to dev-shared only:
  - In each dev namespace: egress allowed to namespaceSelector ns=dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: ingress allowed from namespaces with ns in {dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie}
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No egress from dev namespaces to staging/prod
  - Staging/prod only intra-namespace + DNS egress; no cross-env traffic

5) Default Deny Coverage
- Applied to all non-system namespaces; no policies added to kube-system or other system namespaces

Notes and verification
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-K, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebindings,sa,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings,resourcequota,networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy; kubectl -n prod get networkpolicy
- ServiceAccount tokens: on Kubernetes 1.24+, use projected tokens (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or set up workload mounts as needed.

If you want, I can export all applied manifests in a single YAML bundle for version control.

outputSteps.content:
All requested resources have been created and applied. Summary of what’s set up:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Labels added (e.g., ns: <namespace>) to support NetworkPolicy selectors

2) RBAC
- Per-developer full access to own namespace:
  - RoleBindings (namespace-admin) bind:
    - User alice → dev-alice (ClusterRole admin)
    - User bob → dev-bob (ClusterRole admin)
    - User charlie → dev-charlie (ClusterRole admin)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding (dev-readers) in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - RoleRef: ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod: no developer bindings created (accessible only to cluster-admins)
- ServiceAccounts created:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
  - Each SA has full access in its own namespace and read-only in dev-shared

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - CPU: requests 2, limits 2
  - Memory: requests 4Gi, limits 4Gi
  - Pods: 10
  - Services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - CPU: requests 4, limits 4
  - Memory: requests 8Gi, limits 8Gi
  - Pods: 20
  - Services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - CPU: requests 8, limits 8
  - Memory: requests 16Gi, limits 16Gi
  - Pods: 50
  - Services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) for: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Allow intra-namespace + DNS/system services:
  - In each namespace above: allow ingress from same namespace, and egress to:
    - Same namespace pods
    - kube-system/kube-dns on TCP/UDP 53
- Dev access to dev-shared only:
  - In each dev namespace: egress allowed to namespaceSelector ns=dev-shared
  - In dev-shared: ingress allowed from namespaces with ns in {dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie}
- Staging/prod isolation:
  - No egress from dev namespaces to staging/prod
  - Staging/prod only intra-namespace + DNS egress; no cross-env traffic

5) Default Deny Coverage
- Applied to all non-system namespaces; no policies added to kube-system or other system namespaces

Notes and verification
- NetworkPolicies require a CNI that enforces them (e.g., Calico, Cilium, OVN-K, Weave Net). Verify your CNI supports NetworkPolicy.
- Verify:
  - kubectl get ns
  - kubectl -n dev-alice get rolebindings,sa,resourcequota
  - kubectl -n dev-shared get rolebindings,resourcequota,networkpolicy
  - kubectl -n staging get networkpolicy; kubectl -n prod get networkpolicy
- ServiceAccount tokens: on Kubernetes 1.24+, use projected tokens (kubectl create token <sa> -n <ns>) or set up workload mounts as needed.

If you want, I can export all applied manifests in a single YAML bundle for version control.
